prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Troops in Jamaica captured an armed man Monday who had barged onto a Canadian airliner, robbed passengers and held six crew members hostage, Jamaica Information Minister Daryl Vaz said. A hostage-taker commandeered a CanJet flight at Sangster International Airport in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The crew members were not harmed, Vaz said. The hijacking suspect, described as a "mentally challenged" man in his 20s, had demanded that the Boeing 737 be flown to Cuba. The military captured him around 7 a.m. local time. The FBI helped Jamaican authorities handle the situation at the Jamaican government's request, a U.S. government source told CNN. The CanJet flight from Halifax, Canada, had made a scheduled landing at Sangster International Airport in the Jamaican resort city of Montego Bay and was scheduled to continue to Santa Clara, Cuba. Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who was in Jamaica, told reporters that he planned to travel to Montego Bay to meet with Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding. Harper has been following the airplane security breach and may meet with the plane's crew later today. "The hijacking is that from a mentally challenged youngster and not anything that would be of concern in terms of an international incident," Vaz said. The suspect gained access to the plane Sunday night through the terminal in "a breach of security" that "will be investigated," Deputy Police Commissioner Owen Ellington told CNN. The gunman fired a shot in the boarding bridge as he entered, said CanJet Airlines Vice President Kent Woodside. No one was hit. CanJet Flight 918 was carrying 174 passengers and eight crew members, Woodside said. All the passengers were Canadian, he said. The suspect took an undisclosed number of passengers and crew members hostage before releasing all the passengers and two crew members, said Elizabeth Scotton, a spokeswoman for the company that manages the airport. Two of the six crew members who remained inside the plane Monday locked themselves in the cockpit, Vaz said. The suspect's father and Golding, who flew in by helicopter, were among those who negotiated with the gunman before his capture. The country's minister of national security also was at hand. The released passengers were taken to a hotel, and the airport was shut down for a time, Vaz said. The airport reopened shortly after the standoff, Woodside said. A CanJet airliner was on its way to Jamaica, he said, to take passengers on to Cuba or back to Canada. Christian Gosselin, a passenger on the flight, told his father that the gunman demanded cash from the plane's occupants. Vaz confirmed the account. "The guy wanted to have all their money," said Gosselin's father, Alphonse. "He [my son] told his girlfriend to take all the money and just take her passport and credit card and put it in her back pocket." Christian Gosselin was part of a 25-person wedding party headed to Cuba. He and his girlfriend were released by the hostage-taker, and they spoke to his father in New Brunswick, Canada, while waiting for another flight. "I didn't ask them too many questions; I was more concerned for their safety," the father said. "They were a bit shaken up. It was quite an experience." Another passenger, Brenda Grenier, called her husband and said the man apparently got aboard the plane as airport workers were loading bags. Grenier and her daughter were safe, her husband said by phone from his home in Nova Scotia, Canada. CNN's Joyce Joseph, Janet DiGiacomo, Jessica Jordan, Saeed Ahmed and Mike Brooks contributed to this report.

## Jamaican troops capture gunman after CanJet jet seizure

**MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica —** Jamaican security forces captured an armed man who commandeered a CanJet Boeing 737 at Sangster International Airport, robbed passengers and held crew members hostage before releasing them unharmed, authorities said.

The overnight standoff began after the man forced his way aboard CanJet Flight 918 as it prepared to depart Montego Bay for Cuba and then Canada. Armed with a handgun, he demanded to be flown to Cuba and took money and other valuables from some of the passengers, according to police and witness accounts.

Authorities identified the suspect as 20-year-old Jamaican Stephen Fray. Members of his family said he had experienced mental-health problems, although officials had not announced a formal medical diagnosis. Police said they were investigating how he entered the secured airport area and reached the aircraft with a weapon.

The plane was carrying more than 160 passengers, most of them Canadians, as well as crew members. The gunman released the travelers during negotiations but continued to detain several crew members inside the aircraft.

Jamaican soldiers and police surrounded the Boeing 737 on the airport apron while negotiators maintained contact with the suspect. Security forces eventually stormed the jet and arrested him. No passengers or crew members were seriously injured, officials said.

A shot was reportedly fired during the initial takeover, but authorities said there was no indication that anyone aboard had been struck. The aircraft remained on the ground throughout the incident.

Passengers described a frightening and confused scene as the gunman moved through the cabin and demanded cash. After being freed, the travelers were taken to a secure area of the airport, where officials checked their identities and arranged assistance, lodging and onward transportation.

CanJet said its priority was the safety of the passengers and crew and that it was cooperating fully with Jamaican and Canadian authorities. The Canadian charter airline also sent personnel to assist those affected.

Jamaican officials opened a broad security review focused on how the armed man passed through airport controls. Sangster International Airport is one of the Caribbean’s busiest tourism gateways, serving Montego Bay and Jamaica’s north-coast resorts.

Fray was taken into custody for questioning and was expected to face charges connected with hijacking, robbery, firearms offenses and the detention of passengers and crew. Authorities said questions about his mental condition would be addressed through medical and judicial evaluations rather than assumptions based on family accounts.

Airport operations were disrupted during the standoff but resumed after the aircraft was secured. Officials praised the crew for remaining calm and helping bring the confrontation to an end without loss of life.

**MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica, April 20, 2009** — A gunman forced his way aboard a Canadian charter aircraft at Jamaica’s Sangster International Airport, robbed passengers and held members of the crew hostage for several hours before surrendering, officials said.

The incident began late Sunday aboard CanJet Flight 918, a Boeing 737 preparing to travel from Montego Bay to Santa Clara, Cuba. The flight had originated in Halifax, Nova Scotia.

Jamaican authorities said the attacker breached airport security carrying a handgun and boarded the aircraft while passengers were on board. He demanded to be flown to Cuba, officials said.

Most of the roughly 170 passengers were released within a short period, some after handing over money and valuables. Six crew members remained aboard until the gunman surrendered early Monday following negotiations with police and military personnel. No passengers or crew members were reported seriously injured.

Jamaican officials identified the suspect as a young Jamaican man and said he was taken into custody for questioning. Authorities described the episode as an isolated breach but acknowledged that the ease with which an armed person reached the aircraft raised serious concerns.

Information Minister Daryl Vaz said the government had ordered a full investigation into security procedures at Sangster, one of the Caribbean country’s busiest airports. Officials said they would examine how the gunman passed through restricted areas and reached the tarmac.

Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding traveled to Montego Bay during the standoff and took part in efforts to resolve the crisis, officials said. Security forces surrounded the aircraft while negotiators maintained contact with the gunman.

CanJet, a Halifax-based charter airline, said all passengers and crew members were safe and that it was cooperating with Jamaican and Canadian authorities.

“Our primary concern throughout the incident was the safety of our passengers and crew,” the company said in a statement. CanJet arranged accommodation and replacement travel for those affected and dispatched personnel to assist them.

Passengers arriving at the terminal described confusion and fear as the armed man moved through the cabin demanding money. Some said they initially thought the disturbance was part of a security exercise before realizing the weapon was real.

Canadian travelers told reporters that the gunman appeared agitated but allowed women, children and other passengers to leave. Several said they abandoned carry-on bags and personal belongings as they hurried off the aircraft.

Relatives waiting in Canada said they learned of the incident through telephone calls, text messages and news reports. Family members described hours of anxiety before receiving confirmation that their loved ones had been released.

One relative told Canadian media that the family’s relief outweighed concern over lost possessions. Others called for an explanation of how an armed intruder had been able to reach an international flight.

Canadian consular officials were sent to assist passengers, while federal authorities said they were in contact with Jamaican investigators and the airline.

Operations at Sangster International Airport were disrupted during the standoff but resumed after the suspect was arrested and the aircraft was secured. Jamaican authorities said additional security measures were being put in place pending the outcome of the investigation.
